John Gross, a colored boot-black of Brooklyn, N.Y., has been put in possession of $50,000 worth of real estate by a decision of the Court of Appeals. The property belonged to his father thirty years ago.

Near Bastrop, Moorehouse Parish, La., recently, Bill Harris, a negro, made a brutal assault on a little daughter of George L. Wilder. He was followed by a mob, and the top of his head shot off.

The sum of $265,917 in silver five-cent pieces has been transferred from the Treasury to the Philadelphia Mint, to be coined into a like amount of dimes.

At an early hour on the 31st ult., a mob broke into the St. Francis County jail, at Forrest City, Arkansas, and rescued ex-Town Marshal Apperson, recently sentenced to four years in the penitentiary for killing Tate Wallace, a brakeman on the Memphis and Little Rock Railroad.

Ed. MALLAHAN, one of the proprietors of the Alhambra Theater, burned on the 1st, says he lost $42,000 in that fire.

An agreement has been entered into between the pugilists John L. Sullivan and James Elliott to fight with small, soft gloves, four rounds, in a twenty-four foot ring, December 9, either in Chicago, Milwaukee, or Pittsburg. Sullivan agrees to give Elliott $500 and the gate receipts if he does not knock him (Elliott) out of time before the expiration of the four rounds.

Five Texas farmers returning home recently, were robbed by highwaymen at the point of a pistol.

POSTMASTER GENERAL HOWE has made an order giving Postmasters discretion in returning letters to writers upon application and production of proper proof. Heretofore this power was only vested in the Postmaster General.

At a political meeting in the stockyards, at Chicago, on the 2d, a temporary platform containing a large number of persons fell. A dozen or more were injured, five or six quite seriously, two or three having arms and legs broken. Patrick McNearey had his head crushed, and it is thought will die.

IN THE CASE OF Dick Liddell, on trial at Huntsville, Ala., for conspiracy in connection with the Muscle Shoals, Alabama, robbery, committed by Frank and Jesse James and Bill Ryan, the court suspended sentence and accepted $1,500 bond for the prisoner's appearance next term. This action is said to be taken to avoid fixing on Liddell the imputation of a sentence and conviction, as he is a valuable witness in several other cases against the James gang, and may also be needed at Huntsville to testify against Frank James should the latter be put on trial for the Muscle Shoals robbery. It is expected Liddell will, for this reason, either receive pardon or his sentence be indefinitely postponed.

A MUTINY occurred on the schooner Dora S. Trimble, on the 2d, as she was proceeding outward from Boston. Handspikes and clubs were freely used by the crew, and the captain and mate were seriously injured. The vessel was boarded by harbor police, and two ringleaders arrested.

MAJOR JOHN R. ALLEN, commanding the State troops in charge of the murderers, Neal and Craft, has submitted his report of the fight with the mob at Ashland, Kentucky. He claims that five of his men were slightly wounded, and that the troops did not resent the approach of the mob until after two volleys had been fired upon them.

The annual report of Edward Clark, architect of the United States Capitol, shows that the amount expended for the Capitol extension during the last fiscal year was $57,000; for lighting the Capitol and grounds, $30,000; for care and improvement of the same, $60,000; for extension of the Government Printing Office, $40,000; enlarging the Washington Court House, $117,000.

On the evening of the 2d a loaded car broke loose on the inclined plane at the McIntyre coal mine, twenty-five miles from Williamsport, Pa., on the Northern Central Railway, and rushed down with fearful velocity. A number of men were on the car, three of whom were killed, and two so badly injured that they are not expected to live. The killed are James Dougherty, John Harris, and Lewis Williams; the wounded are John Lundy, Sr., and John Lundy, Jr. Dougherty leaves a large family.

FRED. Hutchinson, of Easton, Maine, cut his wife's throat and then his own on the 3d. Both died in a short time. Hutchinson was thirty-eight years old, and subject to fits, in one of which he may have committed the double crime. No other cause is known.

MISS MARIE NEFFE, aged eighteen, went into the woods, near Chippewa Falls, Wisconsin, on the 3d, to gather tamarack gum. Not returning, 100 people searched and found a portion of her body. She had been deyoured by bears after a terrible struggle.

In a quarrel at Pleasonton, Texas, on the 3d, between Charles McKinney, a State Ranger, and Joe Tomlinson, Sheriff of DeWitt County, both were mortally wounded.

Deadly Assault and Robbery in the Streets of Des Moines Last Night.
THE PERPETRATOR CAUGHT AND JAILED.
A Mob Invades the Jail With Intent to Execute Summary Justice.
THE PRISONER SENT TO THE COUNTRY.
A St. Paul Italian Knifed by His Wife In Milwaukee.
Mob Law In Iowa.

DesMoines, Iowa, Sept. 16.—Jno. James, a grocer, was assaulted this afternoon in his store and knocked down with a slung shot and robbed of $900. While the assailant was stooping over the prostrate form of his victim, rifling his pockets, a customer came, gave chase and after four or five blocks the villain was captured and jailed. Mr. James is said to be dying, and a strong sentiment is growing in favor of lynching the assailant, who answers closely the description of the man who assaulted a saloon keeper last Wednesday night. This makes the third assault for purposes of robbery within a week, one victim being dead and two others probably dying. At this hour (8 p. m.) the streets are filled with excited knots of men discussing the event, and many urging hanging the assailant. A meeting of law-abiding citizens is being got together, and arrangements will be made to secuer best talkers to dissuade the mob in case one is formed.

Later—A crowd of 1,000 or 1,500 men have been to the jail and crowding down through the halls to the rooms in the basement where the prisoner was at first confined, demanded of the sheriff that he be produced. Sheriff Littleton mounted a box and pledged his honor the man was not there, and had heen taken elsewhere. The crowd grew more boisterous at this, and the sheriff, fearing they would batter down the doors and let all the prisoners out, agreed to have a committee of ten men appointed by the mob to go with him through the jail and show them the prisoner was not there. This was done, and one of the men, who aided in the pursuit and capture of Harris was one of the committee. They then passed through the jail and all the rooms and cells, and came out and reported he was not in the jail. Then a cry was raised that he had been taken to the state arsenal. The mob have just gone there. It is said by officials he will not be found there, and has been sent out of the city under a strong guard. The city is intensely exited, and there is little doubt the man will be lynched if he can be found. This is the third assault of this kind in ten days, all made with an iron fish plate. It is now thought this man committed all of them.

Des Moines, Iowa, midnight.—The mob did not find Harris at the arsenal, and returned to the court house, where they hung about the jail, they believing the man was there concealed in some of the vaults of the county officers. The crowd has largely dispersed, although many knots of men are about the streets. It is stated now the sheriff got Harris out in the country in a carriage at 8 o'clock in charge of two men, with orders to shoot him if he should attempt to escape.

DES MOINES STIRRED.
The Last of a Series of Bold Crimes-A Villain Likely to be Lynched.
DES MOINES, IOWA, September 16.—John James, a grocer, doing business at the corner of Twelfth and Sycamore streets, was assaulted this afternoon about 3 o'clock in his store, and robbed of $900. While his assailant, who was armed with a slungshot, was stooping over the prostrate form of his victim rifling his pockets, a customer came in. The villain attempted to escape, but after a chase of four or five blocks was captured and is now in jail. James is said to be dying, and a strong sentiment is growing in favor of lynching his assailant, who answers closely to the description of a man who assaulted the saloon keeper Hans Kastberg last Wednesday night. This makes the third assault for the purpose of robbery within a week. At this hour, 8 p. m., the streets are filled with knots of excited men discussing the event, and many are urging the hanging of the assailant. A meeting of law abiding citizens is being got together, and arrangements have been made to secure the best talkers to dissuade the mob in case one is formed.

DES MOINES, September 17.—A crowd of one hundred and fifty men gathered at the jail and demanded the surrender of Harris, who was captured in the act of robbing James, the grocer, whom he had nearly murdered with a slungshot. Fearing that the jail would be wrecked and all the prisoners released, the jailer asked the committee of two who knew Harris to search the jail for him, at the same time protesting that Harris had been removed. The committee examined the jail thoroughly without finding Harris. The committee, however, continued the search in the neighborhood till daylight.

Iowa.
A Burglar's Visit—The Robber Captured and His Life Threatened by a Mob.

Des Moines, Sept. 17.—At about three o'clock yesterday afternoon a stranger entered the retail grocery store of J. B. James, ocated away from business in the residence part of the city. Mr. James was at the time alone and engaged in looking over his books, and while thus engaged the stranger stepped up and dealt him a terrific blow on the side of the head with a railroad fish-plate bar about eighteen inches long, an inch and a half wide and a half inch thick. The victim dropped behind the counter and has remained senseless ever since. Just as the deed was done the grocery delivery wagon drove up, the clerk came in, and the villain fled through the back door. The clerk gave chase through a number of streets and alleys, and the pursued sought refuge in the rear door of a downtown saloon, when he stripped off his coat and forcibly exchanged hats with a man inside and started out the front way. He was stopped by a policeman and is now in jail. Mr. James will undoubtedly die. There have been several such cases here recently—three within the last week. Now that the guilty party is caught there is loud talk of lynching him.

At ten o'clock the rumor that Mr. James was dying caused great excitement. Previously there had been knots of anxious people gathered in various localities earnestly discussing the enormity of the crime committed and the expediency of letting justice be done without the formality of law. So pronounced had these demonstrations become that at nine o'clock the city authorities closed the saloons, hoping to still the tide of excitement. This turned the idle populace upon the streets, and they commenced to gather around the court house where the prisoner had been confined. Probably a thousand determined men had collected there by ten o'clock. Shortly thereafter a rush for the basement was made. The sheriff and deputies met the mob at the jail doors and declared that the assailant of James was not within, and offered to conduct a committee of three inside for the purpose of proving his assertions. This was finally agreed upon, and a careful search of all the cells demonstrated that the assailant of James had been spirited away by the officers. THE CRIMINAL DOCKET.
The Des Moines Mob Unable to Find Their Victim—Evidence that He Has Been Guilty of Three Murders—Wife Murders and Suicides.
The Des Moines Mob.
DES MOINES, Iowa, Sept. 17.—The sheriff sent Harris, the assailant of James, in a buggy to jail at Indianola or Adell, in charge of two men, at 8 o'clock last night, with instructions to kill him if he should attempt to escape, or if confederates should try to rescue him. The mob remained around the jail here till 2 o'clock this morning, and a small gang staid till daylight. Circumstantial proof now leaves little doubt it was Harris who killed Scribner and assaulted Kestberg, both of whom were evidently struck as James was hit, with a fish plate or iron bludgeon. These deeds of such great brutality, as if the ruffian who committed them delighted as much in murder as in robbery, and were committed with such remarkable coolness and daring that the popular indignation and wrath exceeds anything ever known here, and make certain that Harris will be lynched as soon as his whereabouts can be found, as his identity as James' assailant is clearly established. James is still alive, but the discharge of blood from the brain through the fractured skull still continues, and the doctors consider his case hopeless. He is a man of great strength of vitality, and so may possibly live several days.

MURDEROUS WORK.
A Grocer Fatally Beaten by a Would-be Robber.
Successful Confidence Game Near West Alexander — Miscreants Wreck a Train—The Seductive Concert Saloon.
CRIMINAL NEWS FROM ALL QUARTERS.
Des Moines, Iowa, September 18—Another murderous assault was committed in this city to day. J. B. James keeps an up-town retail grocery in the residence portion of the city. About 3 o'clock, as he was alone in the store looking over his books; a stranger came in and stopped a moment, as he did not desire to purchase anything. Mr. James kept on with his books; when the stranger stepped up and dealt him a terrible blow on the side of the head with an iron bar. Mr. James dropped in his tracks, and he simulated unconscious since. The clerk with the delivery wagon drove up at this time, and the murderer retreated by the back door. The clerk, Robert Faird by name, noticed his hurried exit, and coming in saw the prostrate and bleeding form of his employer where he had fallen behind the counter. Taking in the situation at a glance, he started

In Hot Pursuit

after the retreating villain. He ran him a lively race down town, through various streets and alleys, being joined by several as he ran. The pursued finally sought refuge in the back door of a down-town saloon, where he tarried just long enough to strip himself of his coat and forcibly exchange hats with a party in the saloon. When he started out the front door, the party, who was averse to the hat trade, followed him to the door, and the fugitive was stopped by the police. By this time the pursuing parties had appeared and he was accordingly

March Off to Jail.

He is an active and powerfully built man, fully six feet tall, black hair, and dark, stubby beard. He does not deny the commission of the deed, and the incentive was robbery. Mr. James had in his possession this morning several hundred dollars, and it is probable that this was the temptation. The weapon with which he was struck is a railroad fish-plate bar, eighteen inches long, half an inch wide, and about half an inch thick, and is a most formidable weapon with which to deliver a blow. Mr. James' condition is most critical. The physicians attending him have no expectations of his recovery. The force of the blow laid open his scalp to the bone across the entire side of his head, and probably fractured his skull and ruptured the blood vessels of the brain, as he is

Bleeding at the Ears
continually. There is now talk of lynching. More people are on the streets tonight than there have been at any time since the hanging of Howard, nearly ten years ago.

About 9 o'clock a rumor was passed around town that James was dying. Before that hour numerous groups of excited people had gathered upon the streets, discussing the enormity of the crime and the expediency of letting justice take its course without the formality of law. The city authorities closed the saloons, thinking thus to allay the excitement. This turned the idle populace upon the streets and augmented the excitement. The crowd around the court-house began to swell in numbers and to grow more passionate. About 10 o'clock

A Rush Was Made
for the basement where the jail is located. Sheriff Littleton met them at the jail door. He declared that the man they sought was not in the building. He was willing to show them through the jail, and let them to, and a committee of three was appointed by the mob. A thorough search verified the sheriff's statement. The crowd then demanded to search the rest of the building, which demand was granted. No trace of the man was found. It is known to a select few that before nightfall Harris, as he calls himself, had been secretly smuggled out of the city, but the mob that gathered here to-night declare that they will not let the matter rest here. The object of their vengeance, they say, will be compelled to return here for his trial, and their opportunity will come then. Among this gathering are many of the business men of the city. They have evidently resorted to this method to quell the reign of lawlessness that seems epidemic here. They are in earnest, and will carry out their purpose if such a thing is possible.

A terrible account comes from Des Moines, Iowa, of the attempt to kill John B. James, a former resident of Mineral Point. on Saturday afternoon last, made by a desperate burglar while robbing James' grocery store. At last accounts the injured man was in a critical condition, with little hope for recovery. The perpetrator of the dastardly deed was captured, and had he not been taken to the Winterset jail, forty miles south, in disguise, he would certainly have been lynched, as between one thousand and fifteen hundred determined men had resolved to hang the villain Rob Harris should he be caught.

Last week a Pilot representative was present at the thirteenth annual exhibition of the Southwestern Wisconsin Industrial Association which was held at Mineral Point, in Iowa county. There is a large number of people from that section of country now located in and around Storm Lake and throughout the north-west, and for the benefit and information of those once interested in the "Fairs" of their old home and who still entertain feelings of interest and enthusiasm for the welfare and happiness of the people with whom they mingled in days gone by, we will state that the fair was a complete success in every respect, the exhibition of live stock being particularly large and fine, while each and every department of art and industry presented a good display. An immense number of entries were made, from the simplest product of the farm to the finest and most intricate work of the studio and the sitting room. The races—trotting, pacing and running—formed a decidedly interesting feature, and the Association is now upon an eminently sound and reliable financial footing. JAMES H. ELLIOTT, a New York attorney, has been arrested for entering through a window the house of an actress named Amelia Lanrent and abstracting a deed for property valued at $25,000. It would seem that the woman had locked herself up in order to starve to death.

NEWS NOTES.

John Schengler, of Baltimore, shot his wife and killed himself Saturday.

The Pavillon hotel at Staten Island was burned. Loss, $50,000. Incendiary.

Dennis Donovon, the champion fifty-mile pedestrian of America, is dying in Natick, Mass.

The business portion of Hopkinsville, Mich., has been burned. Total loss, $20,000. Insurance about $13,000.

A new postoffice has been established at Beheet. Platte county, Nebraska, with Herman G. Lueschen as postmaster.

Governor-elect Cleveland has ap-S. J. Tilden, Jr., nephew of Ex-Goveruor Tilden, as alde-de-camp on his staff.

The supreme court of Iowa has adjourned to the January term, when a decision on the prohibition amendment will be announced.

The Presbyterian church building at Fort Wayne was burned Saturday evening. Loss, $25,000; insurance, $15,000. Cause, defective furnace.

General managers and general freight and passenger agents of the lately warring northwestern roads are busy at Chicago arranging the details of east-bound business from Minneapolis and St. Paul. The main features of the agreement are understood to have been fully stated in the recent authorized statement of Mr. Cable. The penalty for violation of the agreement is said to be from $500 to $1,000.

The North Chicago rolling mills at Chicago, one of the largest in the country, which has been partially closed for some time, has shut up all departments. The reason given is inability to get coke for use in the furnaces. The proprietors state that the mill will probably resume work early in January.

The five-story brick, corner of New Washington and Cornhill streets, Boston, occupied by John G. Lovell & Sons, was partially burned a few nights ago. Total loss, $185,000; insurance, $90,000. Lovell's stock consisted of firearms, powder and sporting goods. During the fire several explosions occurred, causing considerable excitement.

The malleable iron manufacturers' association of the United States met at Pittsburg, Pa. Representatives were present from New York, New Haven, Philadelphia, Erie, Cincinnati and other places. The proceedings were held with closed doors, but it is understood the meeting was to consider the advisability of advancing prices, which are not satisfactory. It is not known what action was taken.

The superintendent of the South Chicago rolling mills says that at the reduction in the price of steel rails to the lowest notch orders are coming in freely and the mills will be started up the first week in January, in order to retain customers, even though they make no money.

The sisters of Charity hospital at Big Rapids, Mich., has burned. The sixty inmates were all removed safely. The valuable library belonging to the estate of Father Decunick was burned. Loss not known. Insured for $50,000.

Randall, Bell & Co., of Chicago, have failed for $50,000. It seems they continued to buy corn while it fell from sixty-four cents down to forty-eight and a half and just before prices turned changed front and began selling short, thus getting the worst of it both ways. If the customers for whom they dealt pay up they hope to resume at once.

A Vincennes, Ind., special says that a Mrs. Jones while on her way to her son's funeral was thrown from a train and killed.

The congressional commission recommend that the governors of states attend the Newburg, N. Y., centennial, October next with military escort.

T. B. Gardner, a Chicago lumber dealer, once worth nearly a million, has failed. Liabilities are estimated at $500,000; assets nearly as much. This is his third failure.

Secretary Teller, in the case of the St. Paul, Minneapolis and Manitoba railroad vs. Hans Hansen, affirms the decision of the commissioner of the general land office in holding Hansen's entry for approval.

A Mansard block at Oswego, N. Y., owned by the United States Life Insurance company, of New York, was burned Wednesday night, together with the Union hotel adjoining. Loss, $85,000; partly insured.

Cummings, manager and treasurer of John Whiteley's "Hidden Hand" company, is said to have absconded from Dallas, Texas, Tuesday night. Whitely claims Cummings' cash account is over $1,500 short. He was formerly postoffice clerk at Muscatine, Iowa.

A meeting of the representatives of roads interested in the pool from Chicago through Cincinnati to the south and southwest met at Cincinnati to consider the question of continuance of the pool, but adjourned without action, leaving the pool in its present condition till April 1st.

W. C. Anderson, a Montreal telegrapher, inherits $750,000 from an uncle in Scotland.

The cotton factory at Brownsville, Tenn., has burned. Loss, $75,000; insurance $60,000. One hundred hands are out.

The senate in executive session has confirmed Postmaster James Ruth of Lansing, Iowa, and Jacob M. Bell, of Paris, Ill.

The Texas school fund which can never be disbursed now amounts to the magnificent sum of $114,000,000, including lands worth $110,000,000.
A severe wind and hail storm is reported from Louisiana. Old citizens pronounce it is heaviest deluge of rain since the last inland storm in 1855. Bridges were swept away in every part of the parish. Some cabins were blown down. Travel is seriously interrupted.

CITY MARSHAL SHOT AND KILLED. City Marshal J. H. Spalding, of

Nanahatchie, Texas, was shot and killed by a negro named Charles Smith. The deputy marshal had first attempted to arrest the negro, who resisted and ran. The deputy fired on him. The negro returned the fire. The shots brought Spalding to the scene, and in attempting to make the arrest he was killed. The citizens turned out en masse, and after some further exchange of shots Smith was cornered in an outhouse. The door was forced in and the negro sprang forward and attempted to shoot, but was riddled with bullets.

A DIVER'S LEGS CRUSHED.

At Chicago, as Frank Hills, a diver, engaged in clearing away the ice gorge at the mouth of the tunnel at the lake shore and 67th street, which supplied the town of Lake with water, his assistants in a boat above him noticed two immense ice does rapidly approaching each other in such a way as would intercept the diver's line and cut him off from the world above. They began hauling him up rapidly, and just as they got him partially out of the water the ice floes came together, crushing both his legs, which will probably have to be amputated.

A FEARFUL SNOW AND WIND STORM.

The heaviest wind and snow storm for fifty years has occurred at Newfoundland. Twenty-two vessels were wrecked at Green Bay. The loss of life is fearful.

A RUNAWAY COUPLE SUFFOCATED.

Thos. Doyle and Katie A. Morgan, a runaway couple from Oneida county, were suffocated in a room at Rochester.

ANOTHER FIRE AT LACYNGE.

The farm house of John Clark, at Lacynge, Kas., burned and three small chil dren perished in the flames. Clark had removed two children. and while he was searching for the third the other two wandered back into the house and all perished.

FIRE AT SYRACUSE.

At Syracuse, N. Y., the hame shop of the county penitentiary burned. Henry W. Austin perished. Loss, $45,000; insured.

Annual Congress of the Protestant Episcopal Church.

RICHMOND (Va.), October 23d.—The eighth annual Congress of the Protestant Episcopal Church of the United States meets here tomorrow.

A Clergyman Sent to Jail.

BALTIMORE, October 23d.—Rev. W. L. Woodruff, once editor of the Baltimore Presbyterian, was arrested on a charge of violation of the United States laws by opening a letter sent by mail before it had been delivered to the person addressed. He was sent to jail.

Fatal Fall of a Scaffold.

BALTIMORE, October 231.—Thomas Nugent was killed and Joseph Tinckner probably fatally wounded to-day by the fall of a scaffold, whilst painting a church spire.

Narrow Escape of a Villain from Lynching.

OMAHA, October 23d.—Emil Pepperkorn, the German music teacher who some weeks ago eloped from Calhoun, Washington county, with May Frahm, aged 14, who was one of his pupils, passed through Omaha to-day, en route to Blair, the county seat of Washington county, from St. Louis, in charge of an officer. As the train passed through Calhoun a large crowd gave him a warm reception, and made threats of lynching. He hid in the water closet of the car while the officer watched him, and the train pulled out before any attempt was made. At Blair the train was stopped before reaching the depot, and the Sheriff took a short-cut to the jail with the prisoner, to avoid the crowd, who afterward rushed to the jail, but the prisoner was lodged in a cell in time to escape them.

Frightful Outcome of a Drunken Brawl.
MILWAUKEE, October 23d.—In a drunken affray near Hanover, Wis., Chas. Stewart knocked his cousin, Spencer Turner, insensible with a poker, deluged him with kerosene and applied a match. Following this, he dragged the blazing body out of the house. The victim died Sunday noon in terrible agony.
A Lively Shake-up.
WICHITA (Ks.), October 23d.—An earthquake occurred at this point nineteen minutes past 4 o'clock yesterday. Its duration was about five seconds. There were three pulsations, the first being the strongest, rattling windows, swaying the walls of buildings and moving furniture.
Will to be Contested.
BUFFALO, October 23d.—The will of Mrs. Caroline Fillmore, wife of ex-President Fillmore, will be contested by her Brooklyn cousin. It is estimated that the property will inventory $125,000.
The Georgia Senatorship.
MACON (Ga.), October 23d.—Attorney-General Clifford Anderson will run for Senator in place of the late Benjamin H. Hill.
Immigrants from Europe.
NEW YORK, October 23d.—Seven steamships from European ports landed 4,484 emigrants to-day.

Tarble, Mayor of the city and Collector of the Port, is in an almost hopeless condition. The destitution is undiminished. LITTLE ROCK, October 23d.—The lowlands of eastern Arkansas showed a slight frost this morning, not being enough to damage the cotton. The weather for picking is very favorable all over the State.

ATLANTA (Ga.), October 23d.—General W. S. Hall, of Macon, died in New Hampshire yesterday.

SPRINGFIELD (Ill.), October 23l.—John W. Hiatt, the last survivor of the Illinois Rangers, who served in the war with Mexico, died yesterday at Carrolton in his 89th year.

CHESTER (N. H.) October 23d.—Ex-Governor Ed. Straw died to-night, aged 63 years.

OUTRAGED.
An Attempt to Lynch a Villain Frustrated by the Police.
ELYRIA, May 11.—At about 9 o'clock Sunday night last Miss Eva Broughton, a young lady about sixteen years of age, living on Lake avenue, while returning from church alone was overtaken at the avenue crossing of the Tuscarawas Valley and Wheeling Railway Company by a dastardly villain, who stepped up behind her, tbrew her down, and by choking her and threatening her with a revolver, kept her quiet while he outraged her. As soon as she could escape she fled for her home and, although nearly crazed, told her story and described the appearance of the man. She has since been in a critical condition from the injury and nervous shock. Yesterday a young man by the name of George Wells, an employee of the Elyria Screw and Tap Company, was arrested on suspicion. He was escorted to the girl's house, and she identified him. While he was at the house with the officers, some of Wells' fellow workmen and some neighbors heard that the girl had identified him as the man who had committed the outrage, and they gathered about the house with the purpose of lynching him on the spot, but the officers managed to elude them, and Wells was brought before Squire Doolittle, when he waived an examination, and in default of bail was sent to jail. If he is the man, as now seems extremely probable, it will go hard with him. There will be no lynching, but he will receive no mercy from the court or jury when his trial comes.

Death of a Railroad Man.
TALLAHASSEE (Florida), July 30th.—J. P. Laird, one of the oldest and best-known railroad men in the country, died here last Friday. He was concerned in the building of the California and Oregon road. The remains will be interred at Alton, Il., his old home.

LOUIS, Mo., July 30.—Some time between midnight and daylight to-day about a hundred masked men surrounded the jail at Ironton, this State. and demanded the person of the negro Henry Caldwell, who is charged with criminally assaulting Mrs. Peck, an old lady of sixty years. The jailor refused and did all in his power to protect his prisoner, but the mob forced the doors and took Caldwell out. There was very little noise made after that. The negro begged piteously for his life, but showed little resistance. He was marched to a railroad bridge and made to sit down on the hand rail while a rope was fastened—one end around his neck and the other to the bridge. When all was ready one man gave him a shove and his body went dangling in the air below the structure. This morning at daylight the citizens of the town were surprised to find the railroad bridge so horribly decorated, but the excitement is now all over.

A RAVISHER LYNCHED.

St. Louis, July 30—On Thursday last, a negro named Caldwell attempted to ravish Mrs. Peck, a white woman sixty years old, at ironton, Mo., but was prevented from carrying out his vile purpose by the timely arrival of several men who appeared on the scene in response to the cries of the old lady. The negro was arrested after a severe struggle, and threats of lynching him were freely made, but it was finally agreed that the law take its course, and he was lodged in jail. Yesterday he had a preliminary examination and in default of bail was remanded to jail. This revived the excitement of Thursday, and between 12 and 1 o'clock this morning a party of about a hundred men forcibly took Caldwell from the jail and hanged him to the Iron Mountain railroad bridge near by, after which they fired several shots into his dangling body to make their work doubly sure.

A Terrible Crime and its Reward.
Last Thursday morning, about half-past nine o'clock, we were startled by a cry for "help!" from Mr. Delano, of the Blue Store, coupled with something about Mrs. Peck, toward whose residence Mr. D. started on a run. C. W. Tetwiler, John Phoebe (colored), and one or two others followed immediately. When they reached the residence of the lady in question, they were horrified to see her struggling and screaming in the disgusting embraces of a black brute named Henry Caldwell, who had assaulted her in the yard attached to her house. Tetwiler jumped the picket fence and in the twinkling of an eye, had released the lady from the grasp of the brute. Mrs. P., a lady over sixty years of age, was assisted into her house, while Caldwell was taken into custody, though not without some trouble. He showed fight, and being very muscular would have made trouble for any one single-handed. But there were too many for him to successfully resist, and he was captured and taken at once to Judge Dinger's office, who committed him to jail to await a preliminary examination, which was held the next day. After a hearing, the evidence given being conclusive and damning to the prisoner, the Justice bound him over to the Circuit Court in the sum of $10,000.

The prisoner's "statement" before the Justice was a tissue of the most horrible falsehoods, and those present could scarcely restrain themselves from braining him as he gave it. But everything was done lawfully and in order, and he was taken to jail to await judgment at a higher tribunal.

The feelings of all classes were deeply stirred, and covert desire for a first-class lynching was general if not expressed. The delays of the law, the many loop-holes of escape, and the probable inadequacy of legal punishment were fully and freely discussed; for nothing less than death would suffice to punish the crime and serve as a deterrent to others whose "craziness" might have a bent in a similar direction.

However, Thursday and Friday nights passed without demonstration, and the idea became prevalent that the crime would be left to the arbitrament of law. Public feeling had not abated, and everybody conceded that justice as well as indemnity from this sort of crime demanded severe and summary punishment; but after the sun had twice gone down in safety to the prisoner, the chances seemed to favor his security for the present at least. But the avengers of the hideous lust of the black brute were merely biding their time.

Saturday evening, the streets were unusually quiet, being almost deserted up to eleven o'clock. Then an occasional passer-by was heard on the sidewalks of Main street. At twelve o'clock squads of two or three persons were observed, all coming toward the centre of town, and a short time after, a body of thirty or forty men had quietly assembled on the street opposite Mrs. Moser's millinery establishment. All were masked or had their faces blackened, and were otherwise disguised. There they were "sworn in," the oath administered requiring them to proceed orderly and quietly, and to forever preserve silence as to the identify of all who participated. Then they silently pursued their way to the jail.

Guards were stationed at every corner of the square on which the jail is located, and all outsiders were kept at a distance. Several parties who endeavered to get a close observation of the proceedings were warned to keep aloof, and they were discreet enough to obey the order.

The jail proper is a one-story stone building, with the jailor's residence (a two-story brick) in front and attached thereto. The entrance into the jail is made through a front door in the jailor's residence, which opens into a hall leading to the iron doors guarding the prisoners' apartments. There are two of these doors, with a narrow lobby between, and in this lobby usually sleeps Louis, a colored servant. He is somewhat of a "night

owl," and on this occasion he was still out when the lynchers, headed by their captain, arrived. The front door leading to the jailor's apartments was consequently on the latch, as was also the first iron door. The second, however, was locked, as was the door of the cell in which Caldwell was confined. There were no other prisoners in the jail.

When the mob found its further progress stayed by the inner iron door, an ax was procured, and a man detailed to break the lock. The first stroke awoke the jailor, Sheriff Fletcher, who sprang from his bed on the upper story, and revolver in hand came out on the landing of the stairs to see what was the matter. A half-dozen cocked revolvars instantly covered him, and he was seized by two men, one of whom whispered in his ear: "Bill Fletcher, I am one of your best friends, but, by G—d, we're going to have that nigger!" Of course, unaided, he could do nothing, and he perforce had to let the mob have its way. Thursday and Friday nights Mr. Fletcher, fearing that something of the kind might be attempted, was prepared for such an emergency; but as two nights had passed without demonstration, and public feeling seemed to be somewhat allayed, the precautions had been omitted this night.

After hacking away at the lock in the dark ineffectually for some time, some of the men procured a lamp from the kitchen, and in a short time entrance was gained. Then the key to the cell was forcibly taken from the jailor, and in a trice the lynchers had the prisoner in their possession. A rope, with noose adjusted, was thrown over his head, and they started with him on a run for the railroad bridge. A few yells were given by some of the more excitable men as they passed the Ironton Mills, but these were quickly hushed, and no further disturbance was made until the lynching was an accomplished fact.

At the bridge the work was quickly done. The prisoner was rushed up the steps and to the centre of the bridge, when, the rope, still about his neck, was made fast to one of the projecting beams. He was then thrown over the parapet, but desperately clung to the timbers, when a slash from a knife through the muscles of his arm loosed his hold, and, dropping, he hung suspended by his neck. His feet touched the ground, however, and feeling the hanging might not be effective, some thirty shots were fired at him at short range. The suspended body was completely riddled. The crowd then gave a yell or two, and immediately dispersed, scattering in all directions.

Coroner Grandhomme was at once advised of the matter and at one o'clock in the morning he summoned a jury, went down to the bridge, received the body, cut it down, procured a coffin, and, assisted by Constable Patton and others, brought it up to the Court House, where it lay in the Sheriff's room until ten o'clock next day. Then it was taken to the potter's field and buried: and so came the end of a horrible crime and its terrible expiation.

It was not the first attempt of the kind he had made. During the past few months his actions had been such that he was forbidden to enter the premises of several families for whom he had been working, and the heads of these families had been keeping him under continual serveillance. He had imbibed the notion that he was entitled to a "white lady," and when he was arrested last Thursday, he declared that he was a man and would fight for his "rights." More than one person feels relieved to know that the brute is out of the way forever. We are not an advocate of lynch-law, but if there ever can be a case calling justly for its intervention, this was one. And that's about all we have to say about it, excepting that an example of its swift justice was needed, and to hope that the desired effect will result.

Dr. D. F. Collins, of Minneapolis, Minn., brother of Jerome J. Collins, the journalist, who lost his life with Lieutenant De Long, commander of the Jeannette, wishes Congress to make an investigation. Dr. Collins charges that after the Melville-Danenhower party reached a place of safety, Danenhower asked permission to search for DeLong and his party, but that Melville refused, and ordered Danenhower south, saying he would make the search himself; that Melville soon afterward went south himself without making a thorough search, and remained south until he received instructions from Washington to return North; and Dr. Collins alleges that all the circumstances since developed show that had Melville made an energetic search at the beginning, or permitted Danenhower to do so, De Long and his party would have been saved. Dr. Collins also alleges that the jealousy which existed among the officers of the expedition was such as to make failure a certainty from the start; that entering the ice pack was an inexcusable blunder; that in the retreat inferior boats and instruments were taken and better ones left on board. He also alleges that the provisions with which the Jeannette was fitted out were inferior in quality and insufficient in quantity. Dr. Collins concludes: "Danenhower is anxious for an investigation and will have strong evidence to present. MOB LAW.—When a party of men lynched Henry Caldwell, the act, if not lawful, was not without excuse, and many law-abiding people were and are inclined to overlook it owing to the grievous and horrid jerome which preceded and was the cause of it. Let those who participated in the midnight transaction now show by their conduct that they are peaceable, well-disposed citizens. We want no more gatherings of the kind for the punishment of minor offences. Our citizens are not that sort of people; and will not tolerate mob law, nor subject themselves to terrorism of lawless midnight groups by supinely allowing the administration of justice (!) to be taken up by restless, irresponsible characters who have nothing to lose and may-hap have something to gain in the subversion of law.

The above remarks are in view of the fact that a squad of men is said to have assembled on the streets of Ironton last Saturday night, for the avowed purpose of taking out and "punishing" a citizen whose private and domestic life is alleged to be not such as good, moral people can approve, but suited better to Mormon tenets than those of Christendom. If he has violated the law, and the evidence can be obtained, he will be legally punished, and the intervention of mob law has no excuse whatever. ATTEMPTED HAPE.
[Special Telegram to the Globe.]

St. Peter, Minn., Oct. 14.—Yesterday morning an employee in the cigar factory here, giving his name as Henry Lemke, attempted to commit a rape upon a three-year-old daughter of Nels Wettergren. A neighbor on the premises saw Lemke carrying the child into an outside water closet, and suspecting something wrong, informed Mrs. Wettergren, who rushed down the yard and upon opening the door found Lemke in the act. The villian rushed out and fled towards the river bank, pursued by Mr. Wettergren, the sheriff and others joining in the chase, and upon going down over the bluff found him secreted in the mouth of a sewer. Quite an excitement ensued, and there was some talk of hanging, but the sheriff and marshall conveyed him safely to jail. Dr. Merritt made an examination of the child and found her uninjured.

KILLED AT A FAIR.

Augusta, Ky., Oct. 14.—This evening at 4 o'clock, on the Germantown fair grounds, George Cooper, of Germantown, shot Geo. Insco, of Robinson county, Kentucky, dead. The two had been rivals for the hand of Mrs. Geo. Cooper before she became Cooper's wife. Yesterday George Insco promenaded with Mrs. Cooper in the Germantown fair grounds. Cooper was displeased with this, and said so to both his wife and to Insco. This evening Insco and Mrs. Cooper were promenading again, when Cooper met them, and drawing a pistol commenced firing. Three balls took effect, one in the hand, the other two in the head, and caused immediate death. A brother of Insco knocked Cooper down, and would have killed him but for the interference of bystanders.

AN OLD OFFENDER.

BALTIMORE, Oct. 14.—James L. Carter, arrested in Cincinnati on suspicion of being connected with the murder of A. W. Ross at Glendale, is well known in Baltimore. Several years ago Carter, who, then went under the name of James L. Huff, and was arrested at Hagerstown at the instance of the United States secret service detectives, on the charge of obtaining money under false pretences from the citizens of that place, he at the time pretending to be a secret service detective, and the money was obtained by means of forged pension papers. He was tried, convicted and served a term of four years in the Maryland penitentiary, and was only released a short time since. In June last he reappeared again and visited his old quarters in the penitentiary. While there he renewed his acquaintance with one of the deputy wardens, and obtained a loan of $50 from him by giving him a money order for a larger amount as security, he promising to go to the postoffice with the deputy warden to have the order cashed and repay the loan. He accompanied the warden to the postoffice, and leaving him to wait at the door, Porter went inside and had the order cashed. The prison official waited in vain for his reappearance and upon making inquiry found the fellow had skipped out through another door with the money. After this Porter went to officers Smith, West and Lyons, independent detectives, and meeting D. P. West, one of the firm, unfolded to him a plan whereby he might he might make $10,000. He stated that explosive infernal machines were being manufactured in St. Louis and being shipped from there to New York, to be placed on English steamers for the purpose of blowing them up whilst at sea. In support of his story he exhibited a letter purporting to be from the British minister at Washington, introducing him to the British consul at New York, and promising him $2,000 reward, if he succeeded in working the case up and arresting the parties concerned. Porter proposed that West should advance $200 for expense in New York. West declined any transaction with Porter, and he attempted to enlist other parties, and not succeeding disap peared from this city.

The colored porter, late in the employe of Paymaster Kretz, of the Texas & Pacific Railway, broke a bit of news here Thursday night which was at first not credited, though on investigation it was found that he told the truth. The facts have been kept quiet for the past ten days. At that time Paymaster Kretz went west over the line to settle with the employes of the road. On reaching a station a short distance this side of El Paso the car was halted by an armed lot of laborers who demanded their pay. WASHINGTON, D. C., April 17. John W. Guiteau had a second stormy interview with his brother this evening. His errand here was to get a power of attorney to act for the prisoner in the sale of his book, the procurement of consent, etc. The prisoner was indignant at the suggestions, and said he was able to take care of himself. Small Pox.
National Associated Press

ATLANTA, Ga., April 17.—Considerable excitement exists here over the appearance of five cases of confluent small pox. About three weeks ago a negro girl was taken and died. The cases developed to-day came of exposure to her. The patients are negroes and have been sent to the city pest house outside the city limits. Small pox has been expected here for some time, and the people are pretty thoroughly vaccinated, but it is expected other cases will appear.

Des Moines, Iowa. April 17.—The funer
Murderers Saved from Lynching.
DES MOINES, Iowa, April 17.—The funeral of R. W. Stubbs, the murdered Mayor of Polk city, was held yesterday, the Odd Fellows and the Ancient Order of United Workmen conducting the ceremonies. The procession to the cemetery was over a mile in length. A large delegation attended from this city. Five arrests have been made, and one suspected man is still at large. The prisoners were guarded by vigilants until train time this evening, when they were turned over to the officers. They were taken on board, but when ready to depart the vigilants rallied, boarded the train, opened a switch, placed an armed man at each brake and refused to let the train start. One prisoner was taken off and efforts made to secure the others. Prominent citizens appealed to the leaders, pleading that the law should be allowed to take its course, and they were finally persuaded to permit the prisoners to be brought to this city, where they are now safely lodged in the county jail. It is thought the excitement will die out and that the danger of lynching is passed.

At this juncture the citizens arrived on the ground, seized the two desperadoes. and putting ropes around their necks, hanged them from the Oregon Short Line bridge over Snake river. The bodies were cut down three hours afterwards and buried by the citizens.

Tremendous excitement was caused at St. Joseph, Mo., on the 3d inst., by the announcement that Jesse James, the notorious bandit and robber had been killed at his temporary residence in that city. The news spread with great rapidity and crowds of people soon assembled at the little frame shanty in the southwestern part of the city where lay the dead body of the notorious freebooter whose name had grown to be a terror in the southwest. The shooting, which was done by Charles and Robert Ford, who had long been intimates of James, was accomplished in a cowardly manner, and although the country is well rid of a dangerous character by their act, fair-minded people cannot but harbor contempt for the Fords.

Jesse James and wife arrived in St. Joseph in November last, since which time they lived quietly in the little house where the tragedy was enacted. Mrs. James, who was in the kitchen, immediately rushed to her stricken husband and was loud in her lamentations. Mrs. James acknowledged her husband's identity, saying that she long expected the tragic event which would make her a widow. A ring taken from the dead man's finger, marked "Jesse James" is also taken as convincing evidence that the deceased is none other than the famous bandit. The Ford boys immediately surrendered themselves to the sheriff and made a statement of their action. They said they had been on James' track for a long time. A Passenger Train Boarded at Sweetwater by Brothers of
A Prisoner, John Taylor, They Shoot and Kill Sheriff Cate and Deputy Conway,
Of Chattanooga, Capture the Train and Run it on to Lenoir's,
Where They Leave the Train, With the Rescued Prisoner.

Yesterday afternoon, on the passenger train, No. 2, from Chattanooga, there was enacted a piece of outlawry, assassination and bloodshed, which for boldness and daring is not to be surpassed in the annals of history. In the affray Deputy Sheriff John J. Conway, of Chattanooga, was killed instantly, and Sheriff N. T. Cate, of the same place, was mortally wounded by the Taylor brothers, who rescued their brother, John Taylor, a prisoner being brought from Chattanooga to the Supreme Court, and all escaped. The facts in detail, as far as we can gather them from various sources, are about as follows:

Sheriff W. T. Cate, of Hamilton County, and Deputy Sheriff John J. Conway started on No. 2 passenger train, which left Chattanooga at 12:10 p. m., having in charge three prisoners, bringing them to the Supreme Court, where they were to have a hearing, on an appeal. They were John Taylor, under sentence of ten years for killing Captain John Fletcher, J. L. Carter, white, under sentence of seven years for being implicated in murder, and Ed Bivens, colored, under sentence for robbery. The train was in charge of Capt. N. J. Bell, conductor, and pulled by Engineer Sam. Toms.

At Sweetwater three men took the train in a party, entered the first car, behind the baggage and express car, and took seats towards the rear of the car. Two of the men paid their fare to Lenoir's Station, and the other gave a ticket to the same place. In this same car, about four seats from the front were seated, the prisoners. Two seats were turned together. On one was seated John Taylor and John Carter handcuffed together, one of each of their hands being enclosed in the cuffs. In the other seat sat Captain Conway, next to the window, facing the front of the car, and by his side Ed Bivins, handcuffed to the end of the seat. Sheriff Cate sat in a seat on the other side of the aisle, nearly opposite to the prisoners. No particular attention was paid to the men. The car was crowded with passengers. It was noticed, however, that glances of recognition passed between the prisoner and one of the men.

At Philadelphia, the first station, 7 miles this side of Sweetwater, the train stopped. No sooner had the train slacked than two of the men got up and came towards the prisoners, and the first thing known the man who proves to have been Bob Taylor, the older brother of the prisoner, John, presented his pistol within about six inches of Conway's head and fired the shot taking effect in the left temple and going through and through. Conway barely shied his head, as if to dodge, before the shot. It was a deadly one, however. He hardly breathed, but fell over, with his head behind Bivens, quivered and died. Immediately upon hearing the shot, Sheriff Cate rose up, drew his pistol and fired at the rescuers.

As soon as Conway was shot, Bob Taylor secured his keys and pistol, unlocked John Taylor's handcuff's and gave him the pistol. According to the most reliable information, John then fired and shot Sheriff Cate, apparently in the bowels, which seemed to stagger him. The shot of Sheriff Cate wounded John Taylor slightly in the arm. Some eye witnesses say Cate was shot again, immediately, in the breast, but by whom it does not appear. There was, however, the other evening, on a report of the capture of the Taylors, a wild, unreasoning, mad display of indignation, very inconsistent in a civilized community, surrounded by the laws and safeguards of modern American society in large centers. BALTIMORE, June 4.—About 11 o'clock last night Edward Frames was shot and instantly killed while passing a vacant lot on John street, near Greenmount avenue, by an unknown party, who made his escape. A later report says that Frames was standing on a lot with two friends and heard a woman's cry. They ran to her rescue, and found an unknown man assaulting her. The man fired and killed Frames instantly.

BALTIMORE, June 4.—John Hopkins was arrested to-night, charged with the murder of Edward Frames last night in the northeastern section of the city. Afterward John Degnan, who was with Hopkins at the time, surrendered to the police. Mary Judge, the young woman who was with Hopkins on the street, states that Hopkins assaulted her and she called for help, when several young men came to her assistance. She ran off leaving the parties in a scuffle, and heard four pistol shots fired. An inquest will be held on the body of Frames to-morrow evening.

The Imprisoned Miners Rescued.

SAN FRANCISCO, June 4.—A dispatch from Virginia City says: "Six men penetrated the Alta drift to-night with refreshments for the imprisoned miners. All wore ice helmets, to enable them to pass the belt of 800 feet of foul air between the entrance and the end of the drift. The men were found in comparatively good condition. They had turned water from the drift into their ice-water keg when empty, twisted the end of the compressed air pipe into a barrel of water, and, standing around it, breathed the air thus cooled as it arose through the water. About midnight all were removed from the drift, the whistles along the lode signaling the event. The bodies of Bennett and Callahan, the brave fellows who perished in the attempt to rescue the miners by means of a boat, have been recovered."

Indian Outrages in Arizona.

CHICAGO, June 4.—A dispatch from Fort Apache, Arizona, says: "A courier from Captain Kramer's camp at Forestdale, brings intelligence of Indian depredations, in which one man was killed and some stock driven off. Captain Kramer and citizens went in pursuit of the Indians toward the Cibicu country. Pedro and part of his band of White Mountain Indians were having a war dance when the courier left. It was thought, however, that they did not intend going on the war path. It is believed the depredations were committed by Cibicu Indians and part of Pedro's young men whom he could not control. The courier was fired on and pursued some distance from camp. A troop of the Sixth Cavalry has been dispatched to Kramer's assistance."

Anxious to Fight a Duel.

TROY, June 4.—Captain Twamley and Commander Keith met by chance in the Budget office last night, when Keith said: "I've been looking for you." "Well, I am on hand," replied Twamley, "and I mean just what I said in my challenge. I want you to understand right here and now that I will meet you when and where you say, and give you the choice of weapons. You have lied about me, and I don't propose to stand it." Keith said he would meet Twamley, but did not say when. Twamley being shown a published paragraph this afternoon that his challenge was considered a hoax, asserted that he was in earnest, and that Keith dare not meet him.

The Troy, Pa., Miscegenation Elopement.
THE WOMAN DENIES THAT SHE LEFT HOME IN COMPANY WITH THE COLORED MAN—A TALK WITH HER AT THE DEPOT IN THIS CITY—SUSPICIOUS FACTS IN THE CASE.

Yesterday a white woman of medium size, probably twenty-eight or thirty years of age, attracted notice in the Baltimore and Potomac depot byarrying there a long time and being evidently in an uneasy frame of mind. She was of comely appearance, having small features and dark eyes and hair, and was attired in a dress of gray with brown trimmings, dark chip hat with red and white ribbon, bunch of red flowers and gray feather. She wore a key for a breastpin, had black kid gloves and carried an imitation tortoise shell fan and what appeared to be a well filled morocco purse. She remained in the ladies' room of the depot, closely scanning those who came or went, and inquiring frequently if a telegram she expected would arrive in time. When night approached she took an uncomfortable position on a seat and went to sleep, but whether she dreamed of her friends she left behind in Virginia or her husband and child in Pennsylvania is a matter of conjecture. It was ascertained that she had arrived here on the Midland train, and some ladies who came on the train informed some persons at the depot that she was "the woman who ran away with a nigger." To some who proffered assistance she said her name was Wilson; that she had been to see some acquaintances at Bealton, Va., and now desired to obtain a service place in a respectable family, but if she could not she would go to her parents at Mansfield, Pa. She was told that there had been many publications about her, and the following, which appeared in THE STAR of last Friday, was shown to her:

"AN ELOPEMENT AND EXCITEMENT.

A week ago at Troy, Pa., a black man and a white woman got on the midnight express on the Northern Central railway, and a large crowd in the depot became so demonstrative that the man left the train. It was stated to passengers that they were an eloping couple. There were cries of 'put her off' and 'hang the man' from the crowd. The woman was said to have deserted a husband and children in Sullivan, Tioga county, Pa., who, supecting the elopement, had gone to Mansfield to capture the runaway wife, but missed her. After the man was seared off the woman remained on the trin. Her ticket was to Washington, but she stopped in Baltimore, and was last seen, according to the Baltimore Sun, in the ladies' room at the Calvert station.
The woman denies the story.

She denied that this publication was correct in all particulars, and so focussed at the idea of threats, etc. When questioned by a Star reporter, she insisted that she came here alone and went to Virginia alone.

"To meet the man in Bealton?" asked the reporter.

She hesitated at this question, and said finally: "I have acquaintances there."

"He went with you," persisted the reporter.

"No; I've told you I went by myself," she answered.

"Why, he bought the tickets," said the reporter.

"I don't know," the woman said at first, but then asked: "What if he did?" She further said she left Troy on Friday week and was here last Sunday week, and when asked if she was going back to her husband she wanted to know what could be done with her. When told that her husband was the proper party, if any one, to make complaint, she straightened up and said: "What can he do if he can't prove that the man has been with me."

HER ACCOUNT OF THE SO-CALLED ELOPEMENT.

When asked what caused her to leave, and who the colored man was, she said: "My husband is a farmer near Sullivan, Tioga county, Pa., and this man has been working on the place about a year. He was a lively and talkative man, and my husband thought that he had too much to say. About three weeks before leaving Troy I left my husband, because I could not get along with his people. There was a good deal of talk about this colored man and me, and it was reported that I left my husband on his account, but it was not so. I came away to try to get work, and the colored man was coming on the same train. This excited the suspicions of the people, and I told them that we were not going together, and sent the man word not to go on the train. I did not leave Troy with him, nor did we go to Bealton."

She, however, admitted to other parties that the man bought two tickets in this city for Bealton, giving her one. It was also learned that they did not sit together in the cars on the way to Bealton, that she had come up alone. At 9:50 last night she took the train for Troy, Pa., and it was noticed that one or two colored men sat near her in the same car, but no look of recognition passed.
